body_markdown:
Reports of rising H1N1 infections in parts of India have renewed attention on the symptoms of influenza and the signs that may indicate a more serious illness. Delhi has reported a sharp increase in H1N1 cases this year, while doctors in cities including Mumbai, Bengaluru and Chennai have also described increased influenza activity in some patients.


H1N1 is a subtype of influenza A. The virus can cause anything from a relatively mild respiratory illness to serious complications, particularly in people who are more vulnerable to severe influenza. According to the World Health Organization, influenza commonly causes a sudden fever, cough, headache, muscle and joint pain, sore throat, a runny nose and significant tiredness.


The important point is that H1N1 can initially resemble an ordinary cold or another respiratory infection. Symptoms alone cannot confirm which influenza virus is responsible, so people with concerning or persistent symptoms may need assessment by a healthcare professional.


## Fever can be an early warning sign


One of the most recognisable features of influenza is a relatively sudden onset of fever. A person may feel well or only mildly unwell and then develop a fever, chills, headache and pronounced tiredness over a short period.


Fever is not specific to H1N1, however. Many viral and bacterial infections can cause an elevated temperature. It becomes more significant when it occurs alongside several typical flu symptoms, particularly a persistent cough, muscle aches and marked fatigue.


If a fever continues for several days, becomes particularly high or returns after initially settling, medical advice may be appropriate.


## Cough, sore throat and a blocked nose


Respiratory symptoms are another major feature of influenza. People with H1N1 may develop a dry or persistent cough, sore throat and a runny or blocked nose.


The WHO notes that an influenza cough can sometimes continue for two weeks or longer, even after other symptoms have improved.


Some people may also experience vomiting or diarrhoea, although these symptoms are not present in every case. Because respiratory infections can overlap considerably in their early stages, it is not possible to identify H1N1 simply by looking at one symptom.


## Body aches and extreme tiredness


Flu can make people feel considerably more unwell than they might expect from a routine cold. Muscle and joint aches, headaches and a strong sense of weakness can accompany the infection.


For some people, fatigue can be one of the most noticeable symptoms. Everyday activities may suddenly feel difficult, with patients needing considerably more rest than usual.


The WHO describes severe malaise as a characteristic feature of influenza, alongside fever, cough, headache and muscle or joint pain.


## When breathing problems become a concern


The symptoms that deserve the closest attention are those suggesting that the infection is affecting the lower respiratory system.


Shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, persistent chest discomfort or a noticeable decline in oxygen levels should not be dismissed as ordinary flu symptoms. Influenza can sometimes lead to complications such as pneumonia and, in severe cases, respiratory failure.


People should seek urgent medical assessment if they develop significant breathing difficulties, become unusually confused or severely weak, cannot maintain adequate fluid intake, or appear to be deteriorating rapidly.


Another important warning pattern is when someone seems to improve before becoming significantly worse again. A secondary complication can sometimes develop after the initial viral illness.


## H1N1 can be difficult to distinguish from a cold


A common cold and influenza can share several symptoms, including a blocked or runny nose, sore throat, cough, headache and tiredness.


The way symptoms develop can provide a clue. Influenza often begins more suddenly and is more likely to cause pronounced fever, body aches and severe fatigue. A cold may develop more gradually and often remains concentrated around the nose and throat.


Even so, these differences are not reliable enough to diagnose H1N1 at home. Other respiratory viruses can produce similar influenza-like symptoms, and laboratory testing may be required when confirmation is important. The WHO notes that clinical symptoms alone can make it difficult to distinguish influenza from other respiratory infections.


## Who faces a greater risk of complications?


H1N1 can affect people of all ages, but influenza is more likely to become serious in certain groups.


The WHO identifies young children, older adults, pregnant women and people with chronic medical conditions or weakened immune systems as groups at increased risk of severe influenza.


Conditions affecting the heart, lungs, kidneys or metabolism can also increase the likelihood of complications. For these individuals, contacting a healthcare professional early can be particularly important if flu symptoms develop.


Children require close observation because they may deteriorate more quickly and may have difficulty explaining symptoms such as breathing problems or severe weakness.


## What should you do if you develop flu symptoms?


People with mild influenza symptoms are generally advised to rest, drink plenty of fluids and avoid close contact with others while unwell. Good hand hygiene and covering coughs and sneezes can also help reduce transmission.


People at higher risk of complications, or those whose symptoms are severe, should contact a healthcare professional. Antiviral medicines may be recommended for some patients, particularly those at higher risk or with severe disease, and treatment is generally most useful when started promptly.


Antibiotics do not treat influenza because it is caused by a virus rather than bacteria. Treatment decisions should therefore be made with medical advice rather than through self-medication.


## Prevention remains important


Vaccination is one of the most effective ways to reduce the risk of influenza and serious complications. The WHO recommends annual influenza vaccination, particularly for groups at greater risk.


Regular handwashing, covering the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing, staying home when sick and avoiding close contact with vulnerable people can also help limit transmission.


With H1N1 and other influenza viruses circulating, recognising symptoms early is useful, but panic is not. Most people recover from influenza without needing hospital care. The key is knowing when symptoms are becoming more severe and seeking medical attention when necessary.


**Source and editorial note:** *Independent* report dated 21 August 2026, alongside current general influenza guidance from the World Health Organization. The WHO advises that people with severe symptoms or risk factors for complications seek medical care.
